details:
EMBER (Evidence Map for Burning Environments in Reduced gravity) turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into a fire-safety decision for each crewed habitat: what the evidence supports, where it is missing, and which tests to fly next.

What it does. EMBER harvests all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository through its public API (2,014 test records from 22 different experimental tables) and normalises them into one test schema, with every assumption flagged per record. Pick a habitat (ISS, Gateway, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars, spacesuit or custom oxygen, pressure and gravity) and every view recomputes:

Brief: five evidence checks, each Measured, Thin or Missing, with a verdict. The Moon base meets 2 of 5.

The finding: of 1,735 NASA test conditions with oxygen and pressure, no solid material (fabric or plastic) was ever burned above 22.2% O2, while Moon-base air is planned at 34% O2 and 8.2 psi, and PSI holds no partial-gravity data.

Test-campaign optimizer: exact Gaussian-process experimental design picks the flight tests that shrink the model's uncertainty most across all habitats (five tests: ±0.046 to ±0.037 mm²/s, 21% tighter).

Evidence: all investigations ranked for the habitat with a transparent formula, comparisons, DOIs and test rows. Gaps: every test plotted by oxygen and pressure with a gap-closure planner.

Machine learning trained on NASA data and cross-validated: a Gaussian process for droplet burning rate (257 FLEX tests, 94.6% of held-out tests inside its 95% band) and classifiers for ignition (ACME, AUC 0.74) and self-extinction (FLEX, AUC 0.82). Users can add their own tests and retrain in the browser.

Eight real-time 3D models with physics solvers: FLEX, ACME, Saffire, the glovebox, the flammability landscape, the ISS, a Moon base and a rover. Cut away, x-ray, explode and "break it".

EMBER Copilot: operates the dashboard by real-time voice or text, renders the 3D hardware live, sets the air and runs the models. Ask the evidence: a separate assistant that answers from NASA text only, with verified citations and a red-team worst case.

Why it matters. Artemis habitats will run oxygen-enriched, low-pressure air, which makes cabin materials burn faster, yet NASA's data was gathered experiment by experiment for separate science questions. EMBER shows engineers where they are flying blind and gives NASA a data-driven test plan (directly relevant to the FM2 lunar flammability experiment), so every costly flight test teaches the most. Earth benefits: oxygen-enriched settings such as hospitals, submarines, mines and aircraft cabins.

Creativity and honesty. Instead of a bigger AI model, EMBER is a decision ledger plus experimental design. It never invents numbers: uncertainty and extrapolation are shown everywhere, and assumptions (cabin pressure where a table omits it, concept habitat sizes, upper-estimate spread formulas) are labelled.

Tools: Python (requests, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn), JavaScript, React, Vite, three.js with the Machine Skill kit, Google Gemini API and Gemini Live, Kokoro-82M and Whisper (open-source, in-browser), GitHub Actions, Vercel.
